rv.q: a scathingly funny if not always credible satire by David Ireland making its U.S. premiere at Irish Repertory Theatre.
This is where “Ulster American” starts to collapse under the weight of its inconsistencies.
Ireland’s “Ulster American” is one of this season’s best new plays and nearly as funny as Talene Monahon’s “Meet the Cartozians” and Lauren Yee’s “Mother Russia.”
I smiled through much of Ulster American.
Ulster American , in other words, isn't for everyone, even if anyone is welcome to find offense.

Other viewers are likely to learn a bit about such niceties, linguistic and otherwise, while being amused and perhaps even later appalled by David Ireland’s mordant play, which opened on Sunday in its U.S. premiere.
It’s a marvelous performance sending up the phony pretenses of the artist class.
But it’s Ireland’s intelligent, incisive and often belly-laugh inducing script that wins the day.
The microcosm is powerful and thought provoking.

While he nails the solipsism of a man who’s lived in pampered privilege so long that he’s oblivious to the impression he actually gives, the actor continues his recent run of highly recessive performances capped by unorthodoxly mannered line readings.
What offends about the play, though, is the lack of wit or depth and the easy nihilism.

cn.t: Ireland's provocative satire about toxic masculinity and political correctness in theater earns mixed-to-positive reviews, with critics praising Broderick's performance and sharp dialogue while questioning whether the play's shock tactics land.

vr.q: this was a tight 80 minutes that I ultimately found enjoyable
